title: Context and Diversity Matter: The Emergence of In-Context Learning in World Models
topic: General Machine Learning->Transfer, Multitask and Meta-learning
claim: A single sequence model with shared encoders and decoders is trained on trajectories, then adapts in context and rolls out multi-step predictions at test time.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right: encoders/decoders, training, evaluating; dashed dividers
description: A wide three-part architecture diagram. At left, an encoder/decoder module: observation images pass through f_I into a blue state token s_t. Action icons pass through f_A into a green action token a_t. A decoder g_I reconstructs the image, with an L_I loss shown as a blue double arrow. The middle panel, Training, shows blue state tokens and green action tokens (s1,a1 ... sT-1,aT-1) feeding a Linear Attention Layers band with recurrent states phi_0 to phi_T-2. Hidden states h feed heads g_s that output predicted states ŝ with L_S losses in blue. The right panel, Evaluating, uses the same stack. A chunk-wise computation over the context gives in-context learning. Recurrent inference then rolls out multi-step prediction, with predicted states fed back through dotted arrows. Bold labels and bracketed spans mark the phases.
caption: The world model structure for the empirical study.
abstract: The capability of predicting environmental dynamics underpins both biological neural systems and general embodied AI in adapting to their surroundings. Yet prevailing approaches rest on static world models that falter when confronted with novel or rare configurations. We investigate in-context learning (ICL) of world models, shifting attention from zero-shot performance to the growth and asymptotic limits of the world model. Our contributions are three-fold: (1) we formalize ICL of a world model and identify two core mechanisms: environment recognition (ER) and environment learning (EL); (2) we derive error upper-bounds for both mechanisms that expose how the mechanisms emerge; and (3) we empirically confirm that distinct ICL mechanisms exist in the world model, and we further investigate how data distribution and model architecture affect ICL in a manner consistent with theory. These findings demonstrate the potential of self-adapting world models and highlight the key factors behind the emergence of EL/ER, most notably the necessity of long context and diverse environments.
